title: A Reality Check on Quantum Optimisation: Evidence from an Industrial Case Study
authors: Hila Safi, Karen Wintersperger, Oliver von Sicard, Christoph Niedermeier, Wolfgang Mauerer
abstract: Quantum Processing Units promise speed-ups for selected computational problems, including combinatorial optimisation, but their industrial utility remains an open challenge. We study an industrial variant of the Job-Shop Scheduling Problem using quantum, quantum-inspired, and classical methods across three platforms: IBM Quantum, the D-Wave Quantum Annealer, and the Fujitsu Digital Annealer. By tailoring formulations to hardware-specific constraints, we show that hardware-software co-design is essential for solution quality and scalability. We benchmark all approaches against an exact classical solver and a MILP formulation, evaluating runtime, solution quality, and scalability. Our results indicate that quantum and quantum-inspired optimisation can support industrial solver selection, integration in classical workflows, modelling decisions, and early proof-of-concept development, while suggesting a potential path towards improved approximations for industrial scheduling.
summary: This paper investigates whether current quantum computing platforms can solve real-world industrial scheduling problems by comparing results from quantum, quantum-inspired, and classical methods. The authors conclude that while these techniques are useful for early prototyping and guiding solver selection, achieving high performance requires careful co-design between the problem formulation and the specific hardware architecture used.
main_problem: Assessing the practical industrial utility of quantum optimization algorithms for complex combinatorial problems, specifically using an industrial variant of the Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP).
main_result: Hardware-software co-design is crucial for achieving good solution quality and scalability; current quantum methods are best suited for supporting solver selection and proof-of-concept development rather than guaranteeing global optimality.
method: The study benchmarks quantum, quantum-inspired (e.g., QAOA), and classical solvers against an exact MILP baseline by formulating the scheduling problem as QUBOs.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using formulations for JSSP variants (Single/Multi-Constraint Models) solved on three platforms: IBM Quantum (gate-based), D-Wave Quantum Annealer, and Fujitsu Digital Annealer.
key_observables: Runtime, solution quality (optimality gap), and scalability across different hardware backends.
important_parameters: QUBO size (number of qubits/constraints), time budget for classical solvers, and the specific formulation used (Single vs. Multi-Constraint).
main_assumptions: The optimal QUBO solution does not guarantee the global optimum because the complex scheduling task is artificially split into assignment and ordering stages.
figures_summary: Not specified by notes; focus is on comparative benchmarking of performance metrics across platforms.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares multiple optimization approaches (quantum, quantum-inspired, classical) applied to a real-world scheduling problem, emphasizing the necessary co-design between formulation and hardware.
why_interesting: While focused on scheduling, the rigorous comparison of different physical implementations (annealers vs. gate models) and the explicit discussion of hardware constraints provide valuable insights into near-term quantum algorithm implementation challenges relevant to any complex Hamiltonian simulation or optimization task.
